title: Lecture 4 — Instructor Tutorial
subject: Algorithm Analysis
description: 14 questions transcribed from the instructor’s Tutorial 4: The Master Theorem, divide-and-conquer algorithms, and matrix multiplication. Source questions, choices, and answer-key selections are preserved.

questions.question: Given the general form of the Master Theorem T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n), what do the parameters a and b represent?
options: a is the subproblem size; b is the number of subproblems.
a is the number of subproblems; b is the factor by which the problem size is reduced.
a is the non-recursive cost; b is the recursion depth.
a is the constant time for the base case; b is the number of levels in the recursion tree.
questions.correctAnswer: a is the number of subproblems; b is the factor by which the problem size is reduced.
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects B: a is the number of subproblems; b is the factor by which the problem size is reduced.

questions.question: Which condition must be met for f(n) to be expressed as Θ(nᵏ logᵖ n) in the generalized Master Theorem?
options: k must be a negative integer.
p must always be greater than 0.
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects B: a ≥ 1 and b > 1

questions.question: If an algorithm's recurrence results in log_b a > k, which case of the Master Theorem applies, and what is the resulting complexity?
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects A: Case 1; T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a))

questions.question: Consider the recurrence T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n²/(log n)². According to the provided lecture examples, why does this result in T(n) = Θ(n²)?
options: Because it is Case 2 with p = −2, which is less than -1.
Because f(n) grows faster than the subproblems.
Because the log term in the denominator is ignored in asymptotic analysis.
questions.correctAnswer: Because it is Case 2 with p = −2, which is less than -1.
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects B: Because it is Case 2 with p = −2, which is less than -1.

questions.question: What are the three phases of the Divide-and-Conquer paradigm in their correct order?
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects C: Divide, Conquer, Combine

questions.question: In the context of Binary Search, what occurs during the "Combine" phase?
options: The left and right halves of the array are merged.
The middle element is added to a results list.
No real combination is required; the answer is simply returned.
The indices are recalculated for the next iteration.
questions.correctAnswer: No real combination is required; the answer is simply returned.
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects C: No real combination is required; the answer is simply returned.

questions.question: How does Quicksort differ fundamentally from Mergesort in its "Divide" phase?
options: Quicksort splits elements based on their positions.
Mergesort splits elements based on their values.
Quicksort splits elements based on their values (partitioning), while Mergesort splits based on position.
Quicksort does not have a "Divide" phase; it only has a "Conquer" phase.
questions.correctAnswer: Quicksort splits elements based on their values (partitioning), while Mergesort splits based on position.
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects C: Quicksort splits elements based on their values (partitioning), while Mergesort splits based on position.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity and space complexity of Quicksort?
options: O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
O(n log n) time and O(log n) space.
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects B: O(n²) time and O(n) space.

questions.question: Which sorting algorithm is characterized as being stable, using O(n) extra memory, and having a guaranteed O(n log n) time complexity?
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects D: Merge Sort

questions.question: According to the "Memory vs. Speed" trade-off analysis, which algorithm is "memory-light" but often too slow for large datasets?
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects C: Insertion Sort

questions.question: The classical iterative matrix multiplication algorithm (triple nested loops) has a time complexity of:
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects B: O(n³)

questions.question: Why does the Naïve Recursive Divide-and-Conquer method for matrix multiplication fail to improve asymptotic time complexity over the iterative method?
options: It requires 8 recursive multiplications of size n/2, resulting in T(n) = 8T(n/2) + O(n²), which still solves to O(n³).
Partitioning the matrices takes O(n³) time.
questions.correctAnswer: It requires 8 recursive multiplications of size n/2, resulting in T(n) = 8T(n/2) + O(n²), which still solves to O(n³).
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects B: It requires 8 recursive multiplications of size n/2, resulting in T(n) = 8T(n/2) + O(n²), which still solves to O(n³).

questions.question: What is the primary mathematical "trick" Strassen’s Algorithm uses to achieve a complexity of approximately O(n^2.81)?
options: It reduces the number of matrix additions from 18 to 7.
It reduces the number of recursive multiplications from 8 to 7.
It eliminates the need for partitioning.
It uses an iterative approach within the recursion.
questions.correctAnswer: It reduces the number of recursive multiplications from 8 to 7.
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects B: It reduces the number of recursive multiplications from 8 to 7.

questions.question: Which of the following is a disadvantage of Strassen's Algorithm compared to the classical method?
options: It has a higher theoretical time complexity.
It has higher constant factors and more additions/subtractions, making it less stable.
questions.correctAnswer: It has higher constant factors and more additions/subtractions, making it less stable.
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects C: It has higher constant factors and more additions/subtractions, making it less stable.
